displayQuote: One of the penalties for refusing to participate in politics is that you end up being governed by your inferiors

meta.title: Who really said "One of the penalties for refusing to participate in politics is that you end up being governed by your inferiors"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The idea is genuinely Plato’s (Republic 347c), but the familiar “governed by your inferiors” wording is a modern paraphrase, not a verbatim translation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'One of the penalties for refusing to participate in politics is that you end up being governed by your inferiors'?
meta.ogDescription: The idea is genuinely Plato’s (Republic 347c), but the popular “governed by your inferiors” wording is a modern paraphrase, not a direct translation.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: c. 428–348 BCE · Athenian philosopher, founder of the Academy
answer.sourceLine: The thought is authentically Plato’s — it comes straight from Republic Book 1, 347c–d, where Socrates says the chief penalty for good men who refuse to rule is to be governed by someone worse. But this exact English wording is a modern paraphrase; no scholarly translation renders it “refusing to participate in politics … governed by your inferiors.”

source.heading: Where it really comes from
source.excerpt: … the chief penalty is to be governed by someone worse if a man will not himself hold office and rule. It is from fear of this, as it appears to me, that the better sort hold office when they do.
trail: The passage is genuine: the Greek and its literal English (“the chief penalty is to be governed by someone worse”) are in Shorey’s translation of Republic 347c on Perseus ↗.
A classicist’s post at Sententiae Antiquae ↗ confirms it is a real Plato passage (347c–d) whose viral English form is a paraphrase, not an ancient translation.
WIST ↗ files the “inferiors” line as one of several alternate renderings of 347c, alongside Emerson’s 1870 version and the later “price of apathy” slogan.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular ‘refusing to participate in politics … your inferiors’ wording is a loose paraphrase of this line
source.excerptNote: Greek: τῆς δὲ ζημίας μεγίστη τὸ ὑπὸ πονηροτέρου ἄρχεσθαι, ἐὰν μὴ αὐτὸς ἐθέλῃ ἄρχειν. Shorey’s literal “governed by someone worse” is what the modern paraphrase turns into “governed by your inferiors.”
source.rightsNote: Plato’s underlying text is ancient and public domain. The specific viral English wording is an anonymous modern paraphrase with no identifiable author or copyright holder; quote it as a paraphrase of Plato rather than his exact words.

author.name: Plato
author.heading: About Plato
author.bio: Plato was an Athenian philosopher, a student of Socrates and teacher of Aristotle, and founder of the Academy. His Republic is a dialogue on justice and the ideal state; the line about being ruled by worse men appears in Book 1, where Socrates argues that the best people take office reluctantly, chiefly to avoid being governed by their inferiors.

misattribution.heading: Right author, loosened words
misattribution.intro: This one is not credited to the wrong person — the idea really is Plato’s. The catch is the wording: the viral sentence is a modern paraphrase presented as a verbatim quotation, and it has spawned further variants that also get pinned on Plato.

items.scope: Circulated as a verbatim Plato translation:
items.who: “… refusing to participate in politics … governed by your inferiors”
items.why: No scholarly edition renders it this way. Shorey’s actual translation of 347c is “the chief penalty is to be governed by someone worse if a man will not himself hold office,” per Perseus ↗.

items.scope: Further-mutated slogans also credited to Plato:
items.who: “The price of apathy is to be ruled by evil men”
items.why: A later simplification — WIST ↗ lists it, and the related “good men pay for indifference” form, among the downstream paraphrases of 347c rather than Plato’s own words.

misattribution.truthLine: The genuine passage is Republic 347c–d; the “inferiors” sentence and its offshoots are paraphrases of it, as Sententiae Antiquae ↗ documents.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: In Republic Book 1, Socrates is arguing that the truly good are reluctant to rule — they take office not for money or honor but under a kind of compulsion. The compulsion he names is fear: if capable people hold back, government falls to those less fit, and the good must then live under them.

That is why the line lands as an argument for civic participation. Whether in Shorey’s “governed by someone worse” or the modern “governed by your inferiors,” the point is the same — opting out is not neutral; it hands power to people you would not choose.
context.detailsSummary: On Emerson and the later variants
detailsBody: Ralph Waldo Emerson paraphrased the passage in his essay “Eloquence” in Society and Solitude (1870): “Plato says that the punishment which the wise suffer who refuse to take part in the government, is, to live under the government of worse men.” That Victorian rendering is a likely ancestor of today’s snappier “governed by your inferiors.”

The blunter offshoots — “the price of apathy is to be ruled by evil men” and “the penalty good men pay for indifference to public affairs is to be ruled by evil men” (used on the mid-century Constitution Party letterhead) — drift further from the Greek while keeping Plato’s name attached.
context.pull: The chief penalty is to be governed by someone worse if a man will not himself hold office.
